sub_sections.title: Quality and effectiveness of the work plan, assessment of risks and appropriateness of the effort assigned to work packages
sub_sections.content:
3.1 Quality and effectiveness of the work plan, assessment of risks and appropriateness of the effort assigned to work packages

3.1.1 Overall Structure of the Work Plan

The 24-month European Fellowship is organised into five work packages deployed across a single host institution, Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest, under the supervision of Dr. András Jung. Three WPs pursue the scientific core (WP1–WP3); one delivers the MSCA-PF training and knowledge-transfer programme (WP4); one integrates dissemination, exploitation and management (WP5).

  WP1 — Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state
       Lead: Dr. Rositsa Cholakova | Months 1–14 | 8 person-months
  WP2 — Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration
       Lead: Dr. Rositsa Cholakova | Months 6–20 | 7 person-months
  WP3 — Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration
       Lead: Dr. Rositsa Cholakova | Months 8–24 | 5 person-months
  WP4 — Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge
       Lead: Dr. András Jung | Months 1–24 | 2 person-months
  WP5 — Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management
       Lead: Dr. Rositsa Cholakova | Months 1–24 | 2 person-months

Total effort: 24 person-months, consistent with the 24-month European Fellowship duration.

The scientific sequencing is strict. WP1 must produce calibrated field-state posteriors before WP2 can calibrate an uncertainty-aware AquaCrop model; WP3's field campaigns must begin in time to validate diagnostics from WP1 and the demonstrator from WP2. The confirmed critical path runs T1-02 (Route B proxy architecture) → T3-03 (uncertainty calibration and covariation assessment) → T5-02 (dissemination materials), with a co-equal path T1-03 → T3-03 → T5-02 of identical length. Six deliverables and six milestones with verifiable achievement criteria structure progress monitoring across the fellowship. There are no secondments or outgoing placements; this is a European Fellowship with a single host.

3.1.2 Deliverables

  D4-01 | Career Development Plan                                    | WP4 | Month 3  | Report
  D5-01 | Data management plan                                       | WP5 | Month 6  | Report
  D1-01 | Multi-sensor data harmonisation and diagnostic model report | WP1 | Month 14 | Report
  D2-01 | Decision engine and research demonstrator report           | WP2 | Month 20 | Report
  D3-01 | Field validation and uncertainty calibration report        | WP3 | Month 24 | Report
  D5-02 | Dissemination and communication activity report            | WP5 | Month 24 | Report

3.1.3 Milestones

  MS1 | Multi-sensor data pipeline operational; Data Management Plan delivered | Month 6
      Verifiable criterion: Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, soil-sensor and weather data are ingested,
      quality-controlled and harmonised over the field boundaries on the geospatial/time-series
      platform; the Data Management Plan is delivered as an open-science deliverable by month 6.

  MS2 | Diagnostic method v1 producing calibrated field-state posteriors | Month 12
      Verifiable criterion: Route A and/or Route B produce posterior estimates of the target
      latent field state (root-zone soil moisture, crop water stress) with explicit uncertainty
      over at least one growing season's data; route scope (RQ2) and field-state definition
      (RQ3) recorded as decided.

  MS3 | Uncertainty-aware decision engine integrated | Month 15
      Verifiable criterion: AquaCrop is calibrated retaining an honest parameter posterior;
      counterfactual irrigation simulations run over weather ensembles; the recommendation
      logic selects decisions by expected water-use efficiency under uncertainty, end to end
      from a diagnosed state.

  MS4 | Standalone research demonstrator exercises the end-to-end pipeline | Month 18
      Verifiable criterion: The web MVP runs the full observation-to-decision pipeline and
      presents irrigation recommendations with their uncertainty for at least one field case;
      TRL target (RQ10) recorded.

  MS5 | Field validation and uncertainty calibration complete | Month 22
      Verifiable criterion: Ground truth collected (RQ4); uncertainty-calibration metrics
      evaluated — prediction-interval coverage assessed against nominal (RQ5); Route B
      patch-covariation tested (RQ9); pilot-success criteria (RQ7) applied to the demonstrator.

  MS6 | Results disseminated and fellowship outcomes consolidated | Month 24
      Verifiable criterion: At least one open-access publication submitted covering the
      probabilistic fusion-to-decision framework; open data/models released under FAIR
      principles; dissemination/exploitation and communication actions executed per the plan.

3.1.4 Work Package Descriptions and Task Timing

WP1 — Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state
(Months 1–14; 8 person-months; lead: Dr. Rositsa Cholakova)

WP1 constructs the diagnostic branch of the observation-to-decision pipeline. It acquires and harmonises multi-sensor EO and meteorological data, implements the Route B homogeneous-patch proxy diagnostic architecture, and calibrates a Bayesian hierarchical model to estimate root-zone soil moisture and crop water status (RQ3) as a posterior with explicitly reported, calibrated uncertainty.

T1-01 — Acquire and harmonise multi-sensor EO and meteorological data (months 1–6; Dr. Rositsa Cholakova). Sentinel-1 SAR, Sentinel-2 optical, PlanetScope (access confirmed via the Planet platform and API, RQ8) and ERA5 meteorological reanalysis are ingested over the Hungarian tomato field boundaries accessed via AgroVIR. Data are quality-controlled, co-registered and harmonised onto a unified geospatial and time-series data platform. The QC pipeline directly mitigates RISK-02 (resolution harmonisation failure) and RISK-03 (cloud-cover and dense-vegetation sensor limitations) by applying temporal compositing, cloud masking and vegetation-aware retrieval from the outset. By month 6 the data pipeline is operational (MS1) and the Data Management Plan is delivered as D5-01.

T1-02 — Implement Route B homogeneous-patch proxy architecture (months 4–12; Dr. Rositsa Cholakova, with Dr. András Jung contributing). Route B — the confirmed primary diagnostic route (RQ2) — selects a close, homogeneous patch matched on high-resolution soil and climate data whose biology covaries with the target tomato crop and which the coarse Sentinel pixel can read cleanly, eliminating the sub-pixel disaggregation step that inflates estimation error over small horticultural plots. The control-stand variant, in which a covarying species is deliberately planted alongside the target crop, is embedded so that patch-crop covariation is measured rather than assumed (RQ9). Dr. András Jung's expertise in hyperspectral imaging, field spectroscopy and multisensor-drone fusion, and the Multisensor-Drone-Fusion Working Group infrastructure at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest, are the primary methodological resource. T1-02 is the head node of the critical path.

T1-03 — Calibrate Bayesian hierarchical model for latent field state estimation (months 6–14; Dr. Rositsa Cholakova, with Dr. András Jung contributing). A Bayesian hierarchical model (or Gaussian process — model family decided at MS2 review) is fitted to the harmonised multi-sensor data to estimate root-zone soil moisture and crop water status as a posterior distribution with honest, calibrated uncertainty. Route A (direct one-step probabilistic fusion) is retained as a comparison and contingency route; the route scope (RQ2) is formally recorded at MS2 (month 12). Deliverable D1-01 (Multi-sensor data harmonisation and diagnostic model report) is submitted at month 14, coinciding with WP1 close.

The deliberate four-month overlap between T1-01 (months 1–6) and T1-02 (months 4–12) ensures that satellite data preparation is already substantially underway when the proxy architecture begins, so that the harmonised data layer feeds the Route B model without delay. T1-03 begins at month 6, overlapping with the tail of T1-01 and the bulk of T1-02, so that the Bayesian model calibration can draw on progressively richer harmonised inputs as they accumulate.

WP2 — Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration
(Months 6–20; 7 person-months; lead: Dr. Rositsa Cholakova)

WP2 builds the prognostic branch and integrates it with the diagnostic branch into a standalone research demonstrator targeting TRL 3–4 (RQ10). It runs in partial overlap with WP1 from month 6, drawing on emerging diagnostic outputs, and closes at month 20 with D2-01.

T2-01 — Calibrate uncertainty-aware AquaCrop model with parameter posterior (months 6–14; Dr. Rositsa Cholakova, with Dr. András Jung contributing). AquaCrop is calibrated against the field-state posteriors generated by WP1 T1-02 and T1-03, retaining an honest parameter posterior rather than collapsing to a single overconfident point estimate. This is the project's primary mitigation for RISK-08 (overconfidence: collapsing to one parameter set instead of an honest range), and builds on published uncertainty-aware crop-model calibration methods (doi:10.1016/j.envsoft.2022.105556). The data-input edges from T1-02 and T1-03 to T2-01 are the mechanism by which uncertainty from the diagnostic branch enters the prognostic branch; without them the uncertainty chain is broken. MS3 (month 15) verifies that AquaCrop is calibrated with an honest parameter posterior and that counterfactual simulations run end-to-end.

T2-02 — Implement counterfactual irrigation simulation over weather ensembles (months 12–17; Dr. Rositsa Cholakova). Candidate irrigation schedules are simulated counterfactually over ERA5-derived weather ensembles; for each candidate schedule, expected water-use efficiency (WUE — the confirmed decision objective, RQ6) is computed under the full uncertainty of the AquaCrop parameter posterior and the weather distribution. This is the step at which uncertainty from WP1 and WP2 propagates into the irrigation recommendation, making the output an honest probability-weighted ranking of candidate decisions rather than a point recommendation.

T2-03 — Develop and integrate research demonstrator web MVP (months 15–18; Dr. Rositsa Cholakova). The full observation-to-decision pipeline is assembled into a standalone web MVP. The demonstrator accepts multi-sensor EO inputs, invokes the diagnostic posterior, passes it to the AquaCrop decision engine, runs counterfactual weather-ensemble simulations, and presents irrigation recommendations with their explicit uncertainty. MS4 (month 18) — Standalone research demonstrator exercises the end-to-end pipeline — verifies that the web MVP presents uncertainty-annotated recommendations for at least one field case and that the TRL 3–4 target (RQ10) is formally recorded. Deliverable D2-01 (Decision engine and research demonstrator report) is submitted at month 20.

The sequencing within WP2 is tight by design: T2-01 can begin early (month 6) because AquaCrop calibration can proceed in parallel with ongoing WP1 model fitting, drawing on interim outputs; T2-02 starts at month 12 once the AquaCrop posterior is substantially established; T2-03 starts at month 15 once the simulation engine is in place, ensuring the demonstrator exercises a validated pipeline rather than a placeholder backend.

WP3 — Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration
(Months 8–24; 5 person-months; lead: Dr. Rositsa Cholakova)

WP3 tests the entire observation-to-decision pipeline against real field data and assesses rigorously whether the reported uncertainty is well calibrated. It runs from month 8 to the fellowship close at month 24, spanning multiple growing seasons.

T3-01 — Design and run field validation protocol on tomato farms (months 8–14; Dr. Rositsa Cholakova, with Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest contributing). The validation protocol is designed in coordination with the host institution and AgroVIR, which provides access to Hungarian tomato farms. Protocol design specifies the spatial and temporal sampling plan, the non-destructive measurement instruments, co-location with Sentinel-1/2 overpasses and PlanetScope acquisitions, the seasonal schedule for the control-stand covariation campaign (RQ9), and the statistical analysis plan for evaluating prediction-interval coverage (RQ5). The protocol is designed to be dense enough to detect miscalibration in prediction intervals, directly addressing RISK-04 (sparse ground-truth leaving validation under-powered).

T3-02 — Collect non-destructive physiological ground-truth measurements (months 10–20; Dr. Rositsa Cholakova). Dr. Rositsa Cholakova's specific expertise is the non-destructive evaluation of physiological stress status in tomato; her doctoral research (summa cum laude, 2020; doi:10.2139/ssrn.5492527) addressed the non-destructive evaluation of drought-stressed tomato physiology, with further work on maize chilling-stress photosynthesis and biostimulants. Ground truth is collected using the four RQ4-confirmed measurement types: chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy and leaf temperature, and spectral reflectance. These are non-destructive, repeatable across growing seasons, and directly capture crop water status — making them the most defensible validation currency for the diagnostic branch's crop-water-status component. The control-stand covariation campaign runs within this task, providing simultaneous measurements of the proxy patch and the target tomato crop for the RQ9 statistical covariation test. The 10-month span of T3-02 (months 10–20) is required to cover at least two partial growing seasons, providing seasonal replication in the prediction-interval coverage assessment.

T3-03 — Assess uncertainty calibration and patch-covariation assumption (months 20–22; Dr. Rositsa Cholakova, with Dr. András Jung contributing). Ground-truth data from T3-02 are used to evaluate: (a) prediction-interval coverage — whether 90% prediction intervals contain the truth approximately 90% of the time (RQ5; pilot success = RQ7, the RQ5 target met on the validation set); and (b) the RQ9 covariation test — whether statistical covariation between the proxy patch and the target tomato crop is demonstrated by the co-located seasonal campaign. These two assessments are the empirical core of the project's scientific commitment to honest uncertainty: miscalibration (RISK-06) and unproven proxy covariation (RISK-05) both receive quantitative verdicts here. T3-03 is the critical-path terminus in WP3; its outputs feed T5-02 (dissemination) and close the critical path. MS5 (month 22) — Field validation and uncertainty calibration complete — is the verifiable gate for this task. Deliverable D3-01 (Field validation and uncertainty calibration report) is submitted at month 24.

WP4 — Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge
(Months 1–24; 2 person-months; lead: Dr. András Jung)

WP4 delivers the MSCA-PF structural training and knowledge-transfer programme. It is led by Dr. András Jung as supervisor at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest and runs throughout the fellowship.

T4-01 — Prepare and review Career Development Plan jointly with fellow (months 1–3; Dr. András Jung, with Dr. Rositsa Cholakova). The Career Development Plan is a joint product of supervisor and fellow, submitted as a project deliverable at the start of the action. It documents the research timeline, training plan, competence-development targets and contingency protocols. Deliverable D4-01 (Career Development Plan) is submitted at month 3. The CDP is reviewed and updated at mid-term (month 12) and at the close of the fellowship (month 24).

T4-02 — Deliver structured transferable-skills training programme (months 1–24; Dr. András Jung, with Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest). Training covers the MSCA-PF mandatory transferable-skills dimensions, integrated with the research work plan: digital and AI skills (including responsible use of generative AI in environmental modelling and scientific coding — grounded in the probabilistic modelling and Bayesian inference methods of WP1/WP2); knowledge valorisation and innovation and entrepreneurship (translating the uncertainty-aware decision-support demonstrator of WP2 toward user uptake); research integrity (honest uncertainty reporting as the scientific core of the project); and open science and FAIR data stewardship (the DMP in D5-01 and the open-model release in WP5 T5-01).

The two-way transfer of knowledge is the substantive scientific exchange of WP4. Dr. Rositsa Cholakova contributes plant-physiology and non-destructive stress-phenotyping expertise — the biological ground truth that drives WP3's T3-02 measurement campaign — into the host's geoinformatics group at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest. In return, she receives the host's geoinformatics, remote-sensing, hyperspectral imaging and multisensor-fusion methods and infrastructure from Dr. András Jung's group. This exchange is scientifically productive in both directions: the host group acquires plant-physiological validation capability; the fellow acquires EO data-fusion and probabilistic geospatial modelling competence that broadens her research profile substantially beyond her pre-fellowship domain.

WP5 — Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management
(Months 1–24; 2 person-months; lead: Dr. Rositsa Cholakova)

WP5 integrates open-science dissemination, exploitation logic, communication to non-scientific audiences, and lightweight project management throughout the fellowship.

T5-01 — Prepare data management plan and open-data/model releases (months 1–6; Dr. Rositsa Cholakova). The Data Management Plan (deliverable D5-01 at month 6) establishes the FAIR-data framework for all project data: EO data provenance and access rights, ground-truth data schema and embargo plan, and the open-model release pathway for the calibrated Bayesian diagnostic model and AquaCrop uncertainty model. The DMP is an MSCA-PF open-science structural requirement and its delivery at month 6 is one of two elements verified at MS1.

T5-02 — Develop communication and dissemination materials for target audiences (months 18–24; Dr. Rositsa Cholakova, with Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest contributing). T5-02 starts at month 18 — deliberately after MS4 — because the standalone research demonstrator provides concrete pipeline outputs for farmer-facing communication, and the WP3 validation campaign is substantially advanced (T3-02 data collection is complete by month 20), providing credible scientific outputs for the geoinformatics and remote-sensing community. Results are disseminated to the host's geoinformatics and remote-sensing community and to Hungarian tomato growers reached via AgroVIR. At least one open-access publication covering the probabilistic fusion-to-decision framework is submitted; open data and models are released under FAIR principles (MS6, month 24). Deliverable D5-02 (Dissemination and communication activity report) is submitted at month 24.

Project management is embedded in WP5 and is kept deliberately lean for a single-researcher European Fellowship with one host, one supervisor and one associated partner. Dr. Rositsa Cholakova and Dr. András Jung conduct regular research reviews within the host group. Ethics oversight is integrated into project management: data from human-accessed farm sites and GDPR considerations for farmer-identifying field data are addressed in the Data Management Plan.

3.1.6 Risk Assessment and Mitigation

Ten risks are registered across four categories: data access (RISK-01 to RISK-03), validation (RISK-04 to RISK-06), model complexity (RISK-07 to RISK-09), and operationalisation (RISK-10). For each risk, probability and impact are assessed, a primary mitigation is embedded in the work plan, and a contingency is defined.

DATA-ACCESS RISKS

RISK-01: PlanetScope cost/access not secured, weakening high-resolution coverage of small plots. Probability: medium. Impact: high. PlanetScope access is confirmed as secured via the Planet platform and API (RQ8), making this risk substantially reduced at project outset. The core pipeline is built on open Copernicus Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 data in T1-01, so that PlanetScope functions as an optional enhancement: its loss would degrade spatial resolution coverage for small horticultural plots (where the sub-pixel problem bites hardest) but would not halt the pipeline. Contingency: deliver the diagnosis on Sentinel-1 and Sentinel-2 alone, documenting the resolution trade-off for small plots and treating PlanetScope contribution as a supplementary scientific question. Risk owner: Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest.

RISK-02: Spatial/temporal resolution harmonisation across heterogeneous sources fails or degrades fusion quality. Probability: high. Impact: medium. The geospatial and time-series data platform constructed in T1-01 implements quality control, temporal compositing and explicit resolution-mismatch handling from the outset. Contingency: restrict fusion to the source subset that harmonises reliably; treat problematic sources as covariates at their native resolution rather than fused inputs. Risk owner: Dr. Rositsa Cholakova.

RISK-03: Cloud cover limits Sentinel-2 optical availability; dense tomato vegetation reduces Sentinel-1 SAR retrieval accuracy. Probability: high. Impact: medium. Sentinel-1 SAR is available through cloud cover and compensates for Sentinel-2 gaps; cloud masking and vegetation-aware retrieval are built into the T1-01 QC pipeline; the two sensors' complementary weaknesses are the methodological motivation for multi-sensor fusion. Contingency: weight the fusion toward the more reliable sensor per prevailing condition; gap-fill optical with radar-informed estimates. Risk owner: Dr. Rositsa Cholakova.

VALIDATION RISKS

RISK-04: Sparse dense ground-truth leaves validation under-powered to establish prediction-interval calibration credibility. Probability: medium. Impact: high. WP3 T3-01/T3-02 plan field trials with dense non-destructive ground truth at Hungarian tomato farms via AgroVIR, using a cost-effective physiological sensor network. The 10-month collection window (T3-02, months 10–20) spans at least two partial growing seasons to provide seasonal replication. Contingency: focus ground truth at a concentrated pilot site; supplement with published reference datasets for the soil-moisture component of RQ3. Risk owner: Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest.

RISK-05: Route B patch/control-stand covariation not actually demonstrated, invalidating the proxy. Probability: medium. Impact: high. This is the methodologically central risk: the entire validity of Route B rests on demonstrating — not assuming — that the chosen homogeneous patch covaries with the target tomato crop. The project addresses this risk by design: the co-located seasonal campaign (RQ9), embedded in T3-01/T3-02, pre-registers and executes a quantitative covariation test; the control-stand variant measures covariation directly in the field rather than inferring it from remote-sensing data alone. Contingency: fall back to Route A (direct one-step probabilistic fusion) as the main diagnostic route if covariation cannot be demonstrated; Route A is retained throughout WP1 precisely for this scenario. Risk owner: Dr. Rositsa Cholakova.

RISK-06: Reported uncertainty is not well calibrated — 90% prediction intervals do not contain the truth approximately 90% of the time. Probability: medium. Impact: high. This risk threatens the project's headline scientific commitment: honest uncertainty. The validation protocol in T3-03 specifically evaluates prediction-interval coverage against the RQ5 criterion; the uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration in T2-01 is designed to retain the parameter posterior end-to-end, and the Bayesian hierarchical model in T1-03 is calibrated with uncertainty-calibration metrics built in. Contingency: recalibrate posteriors post-hoc using conformal prediction or recalibration techniques; report calibration honestly and narrow scientific claims to the calibrated regime. Risk owner: Dr. Rositsa Cholakova.

MODEL-COMPLEXITY RISKS

RISK-07: Route A (direct probabilistic fusion) too demanding in modelling expertise, validation data or compute within the fellowship. Probability: medium. Impact: high. Route B (the primary route, RQ2) is a credible fallback in both directions: if Route A fails to converge, Route B is the main delivery vehicle; if Route B covariation fails (RISK-05), Route A becomes the primary route. The two routes are structurally complementary and the inter-route contingency arrangement is the scientific risk-management backbone of WP1. The probabilistic modelling compute runtime is provisioned at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest. Contingency: adopt Route B as the primary diagnostic route, with Route A as a secondary comparison where resources allow. Risk owner: Dr. Rositsa Cholakova.

RISK-08: Overconfidence — AquaCrop calibrated to a single parameter set instead of an honest range, breaking the uncertainty chain. Probability: medium. Impact: high. The uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration approach in T2-01, which retains the parameter posterior throughout, is the direct mitigation. Contingency: ensemble over plausible parameter sets if a full posterior is computationally intractable; propagate the ensemble spread into the decision-recommendation scoring. Risk owner: Dr. Rositsa Cholakova.

RISK-09: Sensor calibration and integration complexity degrades signal quality. Probability: medium. Impact: medium. The QC pipeline in T1-01 addresses cross-sensor calibration systematically, and the WP3 validation layer provides an independent sensor-comparison opportunity. Contingency: reduce the active sensor set to the reliably calibrated core; document excluded sensors as extension points for future work. Risk owner: Dr. Rositsa Cholakova.

OPERATIONALISATION RISKS

RISK-10: Prototype does not reach a usable pilot within the fellowship (operational-frameworks gap). Probability: medium. Impact: medium. The demonstrator is explicitly framed from the outset as a standalone research demonstrator targeting TRL 3–4 (RQ10) — not a deployed or operational system. The scope is research, not deployment; AgroVIR provides farmer access and feedback but does not own or operate the tool. This framing ensures that the TRL target is achievable within 24 months and that the project is not over-claimed. Contingency: deliver a research-prototype TRL demonstrator with a documented pathway to pilot, rather than asserting operational readiness. Risk owner: Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest.

Administrative risk management is embedded in WP5. The Career Development Plan (D4-01, month 3) documents the research timeline, training plan and contingency protocols. Regular research reviews between Dr. Rositsa Cholakova and Dr. András Jung within the host group at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest provide an ongoing mechanism for early detection and escalation of research or administrative problems. The two-route architecture in WP1 constitutes an embedded scientific contingency framework, protecting the project against failure of either diagnostic route in isolation.

3.1.7 Appropriateness of Effort Assigned to Work Packages

  WP1 | Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state              | 8 PM | 33%
  WP2 | Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration        | 7 PM | 29%
  WP3 | Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration            | 5 PM | 21%
  WP4 | Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge               | 2 PM | 8%
  WP5 | Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management             | 2 PM | 8%
  Total                                                                      |24 PM |100%

The allocation is well-calibrated to the scientific architecture. WP1 (8 PM, 33%) is the most effort-intensive WP because it must deliver three sequential and technically demanding tasks: multi-sensor data harmonisation and QC (T1-01), implementation of the Route B proxy architecture with a control-stand experiment design (T1-02), and calibration of a Bayesian hierarchical or Gaussian process model for the latent field state (T1-03). These tasks require substantial iterative development; the 8-month span of WP1 effort reflects the reality that Bayesian model calibration over multi-source EO data for heterogeneous horticultural plots is non-trivial. WP2 (7 PM, 29%) is the second largest effort block, reflecting three tasks each with distinct technical character: uncertainty-aware AquaCrop calibration (T2-01), counterfactual simulation engine (T2-02), and full-stack research demonstrator assembly (T2-03). Together WP1 and WP2 account for 62% of total effort, appropriate for a fellowship whose primary scientific output is the construction and integration of the probabilistic diagnostic-decision pipeline.

WP3 (5 PM, 21%) reflects the substantial effort required to design and run a multi-season field validation campaign: non-destructive physiological measurement campaigns across growing seasons at Hungarian tomato farm sites via AgroVIR, plus the demanding uncertainty-calibration and covariation-testing analysis (T3-03). The 10-month measurement window (T3-02, months 10–20) is driven by the need for seasonal replication, not by the number of person-months: most of T3-02 is campaign execution rather than intensive analytical work, explaining why 5 PM suffices despite the long calendar span.

WP4 (2 PM, 8%) is lean but sufficient because the training programme is delivered by Dr. András Jung and the host institution's infrastructure rather than requiring intensive additional effort from the fellow's research time. The Career Development Plan preparation (T4-01, 3 months) and ongoing skills training (T4-02, 24 months) are woven into the research schedule rather than displacing it. WP5 (2 PM, 8%) is appropriate for a single-researcher European Fellowship with one host, one supervisor and one associated partner: project management overhead is minimal, the DMP is a structured document not a research deliverable, and dissemination activities scale with the maturity of scientific results (T5-02 begins only at month 18 when results are available). The 16% overhead (WP4 + WP5) is at the low end of the range for MSCA Postdoctoral Fellowships, reflecting the focused, single-researcher structure of the project.

3.2 Quality and capacity of the host institutions and participating organisations, including hosting arrangements

3.2.1 Fellowship structure and scope of this section

This is a 24-month European Fellowship (EF) conducted entirely at a single beneficiary institution. The fellowship type is European, not Global; accordingly, there is no outgoing Third Country host and no mandatory return phase host to describe. There are no secondments and no non-academic sector placements. The participating entities are: one beneficiary — Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest — and one associated partner linked to that beneficiary — AgroVIR. The sub-sections below address the institutional capacity and research infrastructure of Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest; the confirmed expertise of the fellowship's supervisor and the precise alignment of that expertise with the scientific programme; the hosting arrangements and mechanisms for integrating the fellow into the host team and institution; and the role, capacity, and project-operational involvement of the associated partner AgroVIR. Detailed organisational profiles and the structured capacity template tables are provided in Part B-2 Section 5 as required by the MSCA-PF application form; this section provides the evaluator-oriented substantive narrative against the evaluation criterion.

3.2.2 Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest — institutional identity, disciplinary environment, and research infrastructure

Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest is the sole beneficiary of this fellowship, hosted within its Faculty of Informatics, more specifically within the Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics. The Institute's confirmed group focus is geoinformatics and remote sensing. This disciplinary environment is not incidental to the fellowship's scientific programme — it is the enabling infrastructure for it. The fellowship's core scientific deliverables — probabilistic multi-sensor Earth observation data fusion, Bayesian hierarchical model calibration for latent field-state estimation, and uncertainty-aware crop-model integration — all require a host whose methodological base, computing infrastructure, and physical instrumentation are aligned with geoinformatics and EO data science. Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest, through the Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics, provides precisely this environment.

As the sole beneficiary legal entity, Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest holds all grant agreement obligations: grant agreement compliance, financial management, reporting, ethics clearance administration, GDPR compliance for the WP3 farm-level data collection campaign (which involves data from human-accessed farm sites under ETH-02), and institutional open-science compliance management. As a higher education establishment located in an EU Member State (Hungary), Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest is subject to the Horizon Europe requirement to hold and maintain a gender equality plan at grant signature and during the grant period, providing the institutional framework for gender equality obligations that apply throughout the fellowship.

The physical and computational infrastructure available to the fellowship is anchored in the Multisensor-Drone-Fusion Working Group, which is hosted within the Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest, led by the fellowship's supervisor Dr. András Jung, and supported under project ELTE TKP2021-NVA-29. This working group provides access to hyperspectral imaging equipment, field spectroscopy instruments, and multisensor drone fusion platforms — the direct technical instrumentation that underpins WP1 Task T1-02 (Implement Route B homogeneous-patch proxy architecture), which is the head node of the project's critical path. The ability to conduct field spectroscopy and multisensor aerial campaigns at Hungarian agricultural sites is a precondition for the Route B diagnostic architecture; the Multisensor-Drone-Fusion Working Group infrastructure makes this capability resident at the host institution rather than requiring external access.

The geoinformatics and remote-sensing group's computing and geospatial infrastructure at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest provides the platform for the EO data ingestion, quality control, temporal compositing, cloud masking, and geospatial harmonisation operations executed across Sentinel-1, Sentinel-2, PlanetScope, and ERA5 sources in WP1 Task T1-01 (Acquire and harmonise multi-sensor EO and meteorological data). The same computing infrastructure provisions the probabilistic modelling compute runtime required for WP1 Task T1-03 (Calibrate Bayesian hierarchical model for latent field state estimation) and for WP2 Tasks T2-01 (Calibrate uncertainty-aware AquaCrop model with parameter posterior) and T2-02 (Implement counterfactual irrigation simulation over weather ensembles) — tasks involving computationally intensive Bayesian posterior sampling and weather-ensemble counterfactual simulation that cannot be assumed to run on a personal workstation within the fellowship's 24-month timeline. The provisioning of this runtime at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest is identified in the project's risk register as the primary technical mitigation for RISK-07 (the risk that the rigorous one-step probabilistic fusion route exceeds available modelling expertise, validation data, or compute within the fellowship).

Administrative support services provided by Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest encompass the full range of institutional services expected of a sole beneficiary operating under the Horizon Europe grant agreement: legal entity registration and management, financial transaction processing, ethics clearance procedures, GDPR-compliant data handling protocols for WP3 farm-level ground-truth data, support for open-access publication compliance, and the institutional framework within which the Data management plan (D5-01) and associated FAIR data obligations are operationalised. These administrative services allow Dr. Rositsa Cholakova to concentrate effort on the scientific programme rather than on administrative compliance, which is structurally appropriate for a single-researcher European Fellowship where the 24 person-months of effort are fully committed to the research, training, and dissemination programme without budget for dedicated administrative personnel at the researcher level.

3.2.3 Supervisor: Dr. András Jung — expertise, research leadership, and fit with the scientific programme

Dr. András Jung is Deputy Head of the Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics at the Faculty of Informatics of Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest, and the designated supervisor for this fellowship. His confirmed research expertise spans remote sensing, hyperspectral imaging and field spectroscopy, and multisensor-drone fusion. He holds habilitations in both Computer Science and Crop Sciences — a disciplinary breadth that precisely bridges the two methodological domains of this fellowship: the geoinformatics and EO data-fusion methods that constitute the technical core of WP1 and WP2, and the crop sciences that contextualise the agronomic target (tomato) and the decision objective (water-use efficiency).

Dr. András Jung is Head of the Multisensor-Drone-Fusion Working Group at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest, supported under project ELTE TKP2021-NVA-29. This position makes him the primary source of the host-to-fellow technical knowledge transfer in WP4, specifically in multisensor drone acquisition, hyperspectral image processing, and field spectroscopy protocols. The working group's instrumentation and methodological heritage are directly mobilised in WP1 Task T1-02 (Implement Route B homogeneous-patch proxy architecture), where the ability to acquire co-located, high-resolution spectral measurements of the homogeneous proxy patch and the target tomato crop is a methodological prerequisite for the Route B diagnostic approach and for the Route B covariation test (RQ9: a co-located seasonal campaign measuring the target crop and the proxy patch simultaneously, demonstrating statistical covariation). Dr. András Jung's contribution to Task T1-02 and Task T1-03 (Calibrate Bayesian hierarchical model for latent field state estimation) and to WP2 Task T2-01 (Calibrate uncertainty-aware AquaCrop model with parameter posterior) is grounded in this expertise.

Dr. András Jung is co-founder of Cubert GmbH, a company producing hyperspectral cameras, and of Brightic Research — engagements that evidence active involvement in the valorisation and commercialisation of hyperspectral and multisensor technology. This valorisation track record has direct relevance to WP4's knowledge valorisation and innovation and entrepreneurship training dimension, in which the fellow is exposed to the process of translating research-grade instrumentation and software into commercially applicable tools. The supervisor's firsthand co-founder experience provides a supervisory perspective on innovation pathways that extends beyond academic publication into the entrepreneurial dimension that MSCA-PF training is expected to develop.

The alignment between Dr. András Jung's expertise and the fellowship's scientific programme is structural, not merely complementary. The fellowship's diagnostic branch (WP1) depends on EO data fusion, hyperspectral imaging, and probabilistic geospatial modelling methods that are resident in Dr. András Jung's research group. Without this methodological provision from the supervisor and the host, the diagnostic pipeline cannot be constructed within the fellowship's resources. Equally, the supervisor's Crop Sciences habilitation means that the agronomic interpretation of root-zone soil moisture and crop water status diagnostics — and the calibration of AquaCrop in the prognostic branch (WP2) — is supervised by someone with formal disciplinary competence in that domain, not merely in the EO methods alone. This cross-disciplinary supervisory capacity directly addresses the interdisciplinary integration demand of a project that bridges geoinformatics, Bayesian inference, and agricultural decision science.

3.2.4 Hosting arrangements and integration of the fellow in the team and institution

The fellowship's hosting arrangements are structured through three governance and coordination mechanisms established in the project's implementation architecture, each serving a distinct integration function.

The Research Coordination Meeting, composed of Dr. Rositsa Cholakova and Dr. András Jung, is the primary operational interface for research direction and progress management. Its decision scope covers day-to-day research direction; work plan progress across WP1 (Probabilistic multi-sensor diagnosis of the field state), WP2 (Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration), WP3 (Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration), and WP5 (Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management); milestone verification; identification and resolution of research risk events; and training needs review and adjustment. This meeting operates at monthly frequency throughout the 24-month fellowship — a cadence that provides the fellow with structured, regular supervisory contact while avoiding the overhead of over-managed meetings for a single-researcher action. Monthly meetings across 24 months provide the granularity needed to detect and escalate risk events early, consistent with the risk management design that relies on ongoing supervisor-fellow dialogue rather than formal committee escalation for routine research challenges.

The Institutional Oversight Meeting, composed of Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest and Dr. András Jung, provides institutional-level oversight operating at quarterly frequency. Its decision scope covers institutional support provision and resource allocation; grant agreement compliance oversight; ethics compliance monitoring; financial and administrative matters at host level; and open-science plan confirmation. This body ensures that the fellow's research programme remains institutionally resourced, that any emerging compliance obligations are identified and managed at the beneficiary level rather than left to the researcher alone, and that the open-science commitments embedded in the Data management plan (D5-01) are monitored against the institutional framework for FAIR data and open-access publication.

The Validation Coordination Interface, composed of Dr. Rositsa Cholakova and AgroVIR, provides the field-access and logistics coordination channel for WP3. It meets as needed per the WP3 field campaign schedule, with a minimum of two coordination meetings during the WP3 active period (months 8–24). Unresolved field-access or data-protocol disputes escalate to Dr. András Jung for resolution, with any issues carrying grant-agreement-scope implications escalating to the institutional representative of Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest through the host's institutional governance structure. This tiered escalation ensures that field logistics issues are resolved at the appropriate level without unnecessarily burdening the Research Coordination Meeting.

Integration into the scientific team of the Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics is further structured through WP4 — Training, supervision and two-way transfer of knowledge — led by Dr. András Jung. The Career Development Plan (D4-01), submitted as a project deliverable at month 3 and co-authored by Dr. András Jung and Dr. Rositsa Cholakova, establishes the research timeline, training plan, competence-development targets, and contingency protocols. It is reviewed and updated at mid-term (month 12) and at fellowship close (month 24). The CDP is the primary instrument through which the fellow's integration into the host's research environment is planned, documented, and periodically re-evaluated; it covers the MSCA-PF mandatory transferable-skills dimensions in full: digital and AI skills including responsible use of generative AI in environmental modelling and scientific coding; knowledge valorisation and innovation and entrepreneurship; research integrity; and open science and FAIR data stewardship. The structured transferable-skills training programme (WP4 Task T4-02) is delivered by Dr. András Jung and the host institution's infrastructure throughout all 24 months, weaving the mandatory dimensions into the active research environment rather than treating them as supplementary modules.

The two-way transfer of knowledge between Dr. Rositsa Cholakova and the host's geoinformatics group is architecturally embedded in the research programme, not a stated intention without methodological basis. Dr. Rositsa Cholakova brings plant physiology and non-destructive stress-phenotyping expertise into the Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics group. Specifically, her established capability in the non-destructive evaluation of drought-stressed tomato physiology — using chlorophyll fluorescence, stomatal conductance, canopy and leaf temperature monitoring, and spectral reflectance, which are the four ground-truth measurement types confirmed for this project (RQ4) — constitutes a biological validation competence that the geoinformatics group does not currently hold and that WP3 (Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration) requires. The fellow's plant-physiological expertise is thus not supplementary to the host's work: it is irreplaceable for the field validation programme. The host group acquires an active, documented plant-physiological ground-truth capability through this exchange. In return, Dr. Rositsa Cholakova receives the host's confirmed competences in geoinformatics, remote sensing, hyperspectral imaging, and multisensor-drone fusion from Dr. András Jung and the Multisensor-Drone-Fusion Working Group, substantially broadening her research profile from plant physiology into EO data fusion and probabilistic geospatial modelling. This exchange is directly relevant to call expected outcomes EO-07 (stronger R&I capacity and better transfer of knowledge among participating organisations) and EO-02 (new mind-sets and approaches to R&I work forged through interdisciplinary experience).

There are no secondments in this fellowship. The full 24-month research programme is conducted at Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest, under continuous supervision by Dr. András Jung. This single-site, single-supervisor structure maximises the depth of the two-way knowledge transfer by concentrating the fellow's intellectual integration into one research group throughout the fellowship. It eliminates the coordination overhead and time-cost that secondments introduce in short European Fellowships — a 24-month duration in which a secondment of any material length (up to half the fellowship duration per SR-08) would significantly disrupt the critical-path task sequence that runs from WP1 Task T1-02 through WP3 Task T3-03.

Support services available to the researcher include the full administrative and physical support apparatus of Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest as sole beneficiary: research workspace and laboratory access within the Institute of Cartography and Geoinformatics; access to the Multisensor-Drone-Fusion Working Group's hyperspectral and drone instrumentation; computing and geospatial infrastructure for EO data processing and probabilistic model calibration; institutional library and database access; career development and transferable-skills training infrastructure managed by the host; institutional ethics and data protection support for WP3 farm-data handling; administrative support for grant reporting and financial management; and the institutional framework for FAIR data compliance and open-access publication under the Data management plan (D5-01).

3.2.5 Associated partner: AgroVIR — role, capacity, and involvement

AgroVIR is an associated partner linked to Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest for the purposes of this fellowship. AgroVIR is a Hungarian legal entity. AgroVIR has no beneficiary status and carries no direct grant agreement obligations; it receives no direct funding from this fellowship. Its involvement is entirely project-operational, bounded precisely to the following scope: providing access to Hungarian tomato farms for the WP3 field validation campaigns; facilitating farmer feedback sessions during ground-truth data collection activities; and participating in the Validation Coordination Interface alongside Dr. Rositsa Cholakova. AgroVIR does not own or operate the research demonstrator developed in WP2, and its involvement does not extend to the modelling, algorithmic, or data-fusion components of the project.

The research-scientific rationale for AgroVIR's involvement is directly connected to the project's validation methodology and is not decorative. WP3 (Field validation, ground truth and uncertainty calibration) requires a sustained non-destructive physiological ground-truth measurement campaign at Hungarian tomato field sites — a 10-month measurement window (WP3 Task T3-02) spanning at least two partial growing seasons, designed to provide the seasonal replication required for the prediction-interval coverage assessment (RQ5: 90% prediction intervals containing the truth approximately 90% of the time) and the Route B covariation test (RQ9: co-located seasonal campaign demonstrating statistical covariation between the proxy patch and the target tomato crop). Access to suitable operational Hungarian tomato farming sites — with appropriate field boundaries, crop management practices, temporal availability across growing seasons, and landowner consent — is a practical precondition for these campaigns that cannot be generated independently by the fellow or the host institution. AgroVIR supplies that access through its established relationships with Hungarian tomato farm operators.

The confirmation of AgroVIR as associated partner substantially reduces RISK-04 (sparse ground truth leaving validation under-powered to establish prediction-interval calibration credibility), which is classified in the risk register as medium probability and high impact. Without a credible, confirmed field-access arrangement, the WP3 measurement campaign would be structurally at risk before the fellowship begins; AgroVIR's involvement converts a project-opening risk into a managed logistical task. The minimum of two Validation Coordination Interface meetings during the WP3 active period ensures that field scheduling, seasonal campaign timing, and data-collection protocols are coordinated in advance of each measurement phase, reducing the probability of campaign disruption from logistical failure.

AgroVIR's role in farmer feedback collection also provides the primary channel through which the research demonstrator developed in WP2 (Uncertainty-aware decision engine and demonstrator integration) is evaluated against real agricultural end-user expectations. While the demonstrator is scoped as a research prototype (TRL 3–4, RQ10) — not an operational product — farmer feedback accessed through AgroVIR informs the dissemination and communication activities in WP5 (Dissemination, exploitation, communication and management), specifically in WP5 Task T5-02 (Develop and integrate research demonstrator web MVP), and contributes to the communication materials targeting Hungarian tomato growers as a non-scientific audience.

The scope of AgroVIR's involvement is precisely bounded and non-overlapping with the beneficiary's responsibilities. There is no ambiguity about which entity holds grant agreement obligations (Eötvös Loránd University (ELTE), Budapest alone), which entity leads the field validation activities (Dr. Rositsa Cholakova as WP3 lead, supported by Dr. András Jung as contributing supervisor), and which entity provides field access (AgroVIR). This clear delineation ensures that the associated partner relationship adds value — providing the field access that the beneficiary does not independently hold — without creating governance ambiguity about accountability. Detailed organisational capacity information for AgroVIR is provided in Part B-2 Section 5.
